newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Tunisia outlines plans to attract funds.
newsitem.headline: Tunisia outlines plans to attract funds.

text.p: The Tunisian government plans new privatisations, infrastructure projects and greater incentives to attract foreign direct investment, a senior government official said on Wednesday.

"For the period 1997-2001, the aim is to attract some 2.25 billion dinars ($2.08 billion), including 1.0 billion dinars in the energy sector," Mohamed Ghannouchi, Minister of International Co-operation and Foreign Investment, told Reuters in an interview.
"Opportunities are increasingly offered to foreign investors."
He said a tender is underway among 10 pre-selected firms to build and operate a 300 to 400 megawatt power plant worth $350 to $450 million.
A second tender is expected to be launched soon to build and operate a 60-km highway between Tunis and the northeastern city of Bizerte.
A third tender is being prepared to involve the private sector in building and operating a sewerage station near Tunis worth about $70 million.
"There are other opportunities with the privatisation programme, with the sell off of some cement factories and some big hotels," Ghannouchi said.

He said that the government will be implementing in 1997 a decision allowing foreigners to buy up to 49 percent of both unlisted and listed companies without prior authorisation, instead of 10 to 30 percent previously.

"This is an important measure which favours mutual interests and the gradual integration of the Tunisian economy with the world's economy, while allowing foreigners to make profitable investments in an emerging market," Ghannouchi said.

"I think that opportunities will be offered increasingly and soon on the Tunis Stock Exchange with the sell-offs of the privatisation programme, with more listed companies and with stricter transparency laws," he added.
"Foreigners are also allowed to own 100 percent of the capital of companies operating in the services sector linked to industry, such as technical assistance and engineering studies," he noted.
He added that additional opportunities were offered by the plan for the modernisation of some 2,000 industrial firms between 1997 and 2001 to adapt them to a free trade zone with the European Union.
The plan itself needs financing estimated by a business association at more than $2.5 billion.
"Several of these firms will seek foreign partnership in their capital and plants in order to ameliorate their finances or to have a bigger access to markets and technologies," Ghannouchi said.

"Of course, there are also several opportunities for the establishment of new activities and services. Tunisia offers signficant comparative advantages in the booming sector of tourism, and in textiles and shoes which have some 900 firms fully or partly owned by foreigners," he said.
These advantages extend also to the pharmaceutical, food, mechanical, electric and electronic sectors, he added.
Ghannouchi said that the government was preparing new hydrocarbon and mining codes in order to simplify and harmonise the legislative framework for direct foreign investment in these sectors.
Industry officials said the codes would be ready by this year.

Ghannouchi said that direct foreign investments in 1996 amounted to 302 million dinars, down from an average 500 million dinars per year during the last four years because of the end of $6OO million investment in the gas field of Miskar by British Gas and the investment in the doubling of the Algeria-Italy gas pipeline.

"If we exclude energy, foreign investments increased in 1996, amounting to 167 million dinars from 99 million dinars in 1995... including a Saudi businessman's investment in tourism and a 12 million dinar German investment in the cables industry in the city of Sousse," he said.
"The accord with the European Union (signed in 1995) has already started boosting foreign investment," Ghannouchi said. ($=1.08 dinar)
